attribution: Grant, L., Vanderkelen, I., Gudmundsson, L., Fischer, E., Seneviratne, S. I. & Thiery, W. (2025). Global emergence of unprecedented lifetime exposure to climate extremes. Nature 641, 374–379. doi:10.1038/s41586-025-08907-1. CC BY 4.0.
description: The share of the people born in 1960 and in 2020 who are projected to live through more heatwaves in their lifetime than all but 1 in 10,000 lifetimes in a pre-industrial climate, along warming pathways that reach 1.5, 2.5 or 3.5 °C by 2100, as Grant and colleagues (2025) state it for the world. It is modelled from the ISIMIP2b climate simulations, and 'unprecedented' is a statistical threshold (beyond the 99.99th percentile of pre-industrial lifetimes), not a count of deaths or of illness. The article gives one value for people born in 1960 whatever the pathway, and no world value for people born in 2020 on the 2.5 °C pathway.
notes: "Unprecedented exposure to heatwaves", second paragraph: "Comparatively, CFheatwaves of the 2020 birth cohort is almost doubled in a 3.5 °C pathway, reaching 92%." Abstract: "If global warming reaches 3.5 °C by 2100, this fraction rises to 92% for heatwaves, 29% for crop failures and 14% for river floods."

"Unprecedented exposure to heatwaves", second paragraph: "In a 1.5 °C pathway, CFheatwaves stabilizes for recent birth cohorts, reaching an average of 52% for the 2020 birth cohort (62 million people)." Abstract: "Under a 1.5 °C pathway, 52% of people born in 2020 will experience unprecedented lifetime exposure to heatwaves."

"Unprecedented exposure to heatwaves", second paragraph: "Of the 81 million people born in 1960, on average, around 16% (13 million people) face ULE to heatwaves regardless of the scenario." The article gives this one value for the 1960 cohort on every pathway.

processing.description: Read the article's JATS XML from Europe PMC (sha256 4224ab518159…), checked its DOI and its CC BY 4.0 licence statement, and found in its text the 3 Results sentences and 2 abstract sentences that state the values, and 10 sentences of the Methods and Discussion that the scope relies on.

Published 5 world shares exactly as the Results text prints them, each read from the words that state it inside its checked sentence: 16% for people born in 1960, which the article gives 'regardless of the scenario' and which is therefore shown under each of the three pathways, and 52% (1.5 °C) and 92% (3.5 °C) for people born in 2020. The abstract states 52% and 92% again; each was checked to print the same number.

Published people born in 2020 on the 2.5 °C pathway as missing, because the text states no world share for it. Nothing was read from a figure or computed, and the numbers of people in the same sentences (13, 62 and 111 million) are not published.

published_value.quote: Under a 1.5 °C pathway, 52% of people born in 2020 will experience unprecedented lifetime exposure to heatwaves. If global warming reaches 3.5 °C by 2100, this fraction rises to 92% for heatwaves, 29% for crop failures and 14% for river floods.

scope.baseline: Pre-industrial control climate (lifetimes resampled from pre-industrial simulations); warming levels relative to 1850–1900
scope.basis: Projected (modelled) lifetime exposure. A heatwave is a 3-day extreme heat event expected about once a century in a pre-industrial climate, from four bias-adjusted CMIP5 climate models (ISIMIP2b). A birth cohort in a grid cell faces unprecedented lifetime exposure when its lifetime count passes the 99.99th percentile of pre-industrial lifetimes there; the whole cohort of that cell is then counted. Lifetimes use each country's average life expectancy, with no migration and no adaptation (such as air conditioning). Pathways are constructed from AR6 scenarios; the 1.5 °C pathway peaks at 1.57 °C. The period is the year of publication; each value covers the cohort's whole lifetime.
scope.geography: World: the 177 countries the article covers, every 0.5° land grid cell

missing_reason: Grant et al. (2025) state no world share for people born in 2020 on the 2.5 °C pathway: the text gives the 1.5 °C and 3.5 °C values only, and Fig. 2a draws the 2.5 °C value as a box plot, which is not read.

title: Share of people born in 1960 and 2020 projected to face unprecedented lifetime exposure to heatwaves (Grant et al. 2025)

unit.label: percent of the people born that year
